Under the proposed deal, Iran would receive sanctions relief and gain access to frozen funds. Iran defends two-day proposal for peace talks after US rejects conditions
Iran defended a proposal on Monday to restart peace talks in as few as two days as the most reasonable offer on the table, after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called some of Iran's conditions "outrageous and ridiculous".
"Is it unreasonable that Iran demands that US illegal sanctions and its naval blockade must be lifted before negotiations start and that the war should end on all fronts?" Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told a weekly press conference in response to Rubio's remarks.
Iran has made the offer to shorten the time to restart talks from an earlier seven-day proposal, which calls for Washington to first meet conditions including halting hostilities, lifting a blockade and waiving sanctions.
Baghaei also said US pressure on Iraq to close most of its borders with Iran should not affect bilateral ties with Baghdad, after Iraq's foreign minister said Washington was pushing for such a move. Baghaei dismissed a US military task force aimed at restricting Iran's land trade as a diversion following President Donald Trump's Republicans' losses in midterm elections.

A sand embankment collapsed on tents sheltering displaced Palestinians in the Gaza Strip late on Sunday, killing three children and two women as severe weather battered the territory.
At least five other people were rescued with injuries by Civil Defence search-and-rescue teams at the makeshift camp in Deir al-Balah, where operations to locate missing people continued.
Mahmoud Basal, spokesperson for the Palestinian Civil Defence in Gaza, said the massive sandy embankment and surrounding mounds of earth collapsed after a low-pressure weather system brought torrential rain and strong winds to the Strip over the weekend.
Two of those killed were identified as Mariam Nabhan and her son, Salah Nabhan. The other three were Reem al-Zain, Habiba al-Zain and Ibrahim al-Zain.
Weekend downpours flooded an estimated 70,000 temporary tents sheltering displaced families across Gaza, leaving thousands of people exposed to the elements.
Palestinians have blamed Israel’s genocide and ongoing siege for the worsening conditions facing displaced people.
“This is not simply the result of severe weather. It is the direct consequence of prolonged Israeli genocide, the widespread destruction of infrastructure, continued displacement, and the denial of essential humanitarian assistance and adequate shelter,” the Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Saturday.
The ministry said nearly two million Palestinians were living in approximately 270,000 tents across Gaza in “appalling humanitarian conditions”.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has dismissed a new US military initiative to restrict the movement of goods through Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea as “merely wordplay”, as tensions over shipping routes and Washington's blockade continue.
“The Iron Gate plan is merely wordplay. The Americans cannot achieve their objectives of imposing severe economic pressure to cause economic collapse in Iran through this approach,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi told the semi-official Fars news agency on Sunday, according to Reuters.
Mohebbi said Washington had previously predicted that Iran would suffer economic collapse within two weeks, but that this had not happened.
Tehran had prepared for economic pressure and maintained close relations with neighbouring countries, he said.
The response came after US Central Command (Centcom) announced the establishment of Task Force Iron Gate on Saturday.

Iran tells Russia talks with US without guarantees won't end conflict, report says
Iran’s ambassador to Moscow Kazem Jalali has said Iran and Russia have discussed strengthening military and security cooperation, with Tehran stressing that talks with the US could not end the conflict without credible guarantees, according to Mehr News Agency.
Jalali said that during a three-hour meeting, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, briefed Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tehran’s strategic priorities, including accelerating construction of the Rasht-Astara railway and completing the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC).
Jalali said Rezaei conveyed Tehran’s position that negotiations with Washington could not end the conflict without credible guarantees, citing repeated "US violations of commitments" during previous diplomatic engagements, Mehr reported.
He said Rezaei also explained Iran’s response to a letter from US Vice President JD Vance, stressing that dialogue alone could not provide a basis for ending the war.
According to Jalali, Rezaei cited several instances in which Iran had come under attack during diplomatic initiatives, including negotiations in Oman and Geneva, as well as engagements surrounding the Islamabad MoU.
The ambassador said Tehran had made acceptance of its seven strategic conditions by Washington a prerequisite for any new diplomatic initiative. He added that Moscow understood Iran’s position and agreed that commitments had to be implemented.

There is nothing particularly unusual about an election stunt. Politicians routinely perform them. Rarely, though, is a stunt as obvious as the one US President Donald Trump pulled on 3 November, Election Day, when he announced that America would, at year's end, stop providing $4bn in annual military aid to Israel.
Trump had clearly read the room, and the polls.
For all his public disdain for polls he claims are "fake" or "rigged", the president understands their political significance.
Polling data suggests that American voters are increasingly uncomfortable contributing their tax dollars to Israel's military, particularly as costs rise in the US and Americans struggle to afford basic necessities.
An August Marquette Law School poll, for example, found that 52 percent of American adults believe Washington provides Israel with too much military aid. Only 16 percent said it provides too little. Even among Republicans under 30, 54 percent said Washington gives Israel too much.

For years, mainstream media has been criticised for its failure to report accurately on Israel’s genocide in Gaza, allowing Israel to commit crimes with impunity.
In July the UN special rapporteur for the Palestinian territories, Fransesca Albanese, released a report about the media complicity in genocide.
Her report details how the systematic targeting of Palestinian journalists, Israeli media’s incitement, and the legitimisation from international coverage have facilitated genocide and obstructed accountability.
Outlets relied heavily on Israeli sources, using the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 to justify Israel’s subsequent onslaught and present the conflict as though it began exclusively with the attack.
It was frustration with this narrative that prompted Maria Robles, an independent researcher and artist, to begin research into archival American newspaper stories.

Several hundred activists occupied the construction site of a planned Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam on Friday, protesting the technology giant's alleged role in facilitating Israel's genocide in Gaza, as well as the environmental impact of artificial intelligence infrastructure.
The demonstration, organised by climate and justice collective Geef Tegengas and environmental group Fossielvrij, halted construction work for the day in the city's Sloterdijk district.

Dutch news agency ANP reported that police arrested between 150 and 200 protesters, while others left voluntarily.
The protest was part of a wider two-day mobilisation across Europe called by the Stop Dirty Data Centers coalition, which is demanding a pause in the construction of new data centre facilities.

UKMTO says 11 ships attacked in week to 4 Nov in Hormuz, Arabian Gulf
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has reported 11 attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and Arabian Gulf in the seven days to November 4, including incidents that left three vessels sunk.
Eight attacks occurred in the Strait of Hormuz and three in the Arabian Gulf, according to UKMTO's weekly overview. Of the 11 incidents, three vessels continued their voyages, five required assistance and three sank.
The report said one dhow was struck by an unidentified projectile on 2 November, killing one crew member, while 13 others were rescued by local authorities.
A Panama-flagged supply vessel was also struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on 1 November and reportedly sank after a nearby merchant vessel rescued its crew.
A Marshall Islands-flagged tanker was struck by two unidentified projectiles in the Arabian Gulf on 4 November, leaving it drifting and requiring assistance from local authorities.
Combined Strait of Hormuz traffic reached 325 transits in the seven-day reporting period, comprising 170 outbound and 155 inbound movements, compared with 277 in the previous week. UKMTO said traffic remained approximately 65 percent below pre-conflict levels.
Automatic Identification System-observed transits increased to 71 from 64 the previous week, while US-reported facilitated transits remained broadly stable. Around 80 percent of Strait of Hormuz transits continued to involve energy carriers.
UKMTO also reported an increase in vessels using the southern route, although most ships broadcasting AIS continued to use the Iranian route.
In the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb, no attacks on shipping were reported during the week. The last reported attack was on August 24, 65 days earlier. However, Bab el-Mandeb transits remained 24 percent below levels recorded before the Houthi blockade announcement on July 22.

The two countries signed the agreement in Riyadh during a visit by Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for the second time in less than a month. The full terms of the deal were not made public.
Turkey, a close ally of Damascus, recently ratified a defence pact signed in Mecca in August by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey.

The number of birth defects recorded among newborns in Gaza during the first nine months of 2026 has exceeded the total reported for the whole of 2022, the year before Israel’s war on the territory began, the Palestinian news agency Wafa has reported.
A medical source in Gaza told Wafa that 260 cases were recorded between January and September, compared with 184 cases in all of 2022.
The source said 322 cases were recorded in 2025, a 75 percent increase on the 2022 figure.
Possible contributing factors include maternal malnutrition, exposure to environmental pollutants and disruptions to prenatal care during the war, the source said, calling for an independent international scientific investigation.
The source cautioned that the figures alone do not establish the rate of congenital anomalies among newborns or determine their causes.
A January 2025 report by Human Rights Watch said pregnant women in Gaza faced serious health risks because of the war, the blockade, damage to health facilities and shortages of food, water and medicine.

A network of 1,653 X accounts posing as Iranian users amplified Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s election campaign ahead of last week’s vote, Haaretz reported on Friday.
The accounts posted messages in Hebrew urging Israelis to vote for Netanyahu “on behalf of the Iranian people”.
The accounts, which claimed to belong to Iranians living in Iran or abroad, appeared to coordinate their activity. Their operators remain unidentified.
Activity intensified on election day, when multiple accounts published identical messages and responded to posts in coordinated bursts.
Two accounts, for example, shared 109 identical posts, compared with just four expected through organic activity, according to Haaretz’s analysis.
They also responded simultaneously, or within five minutes of each other, to 232 posts by 53 different accounts.
